newsitem.title: USA: Big Japan-carry-trade unwindings slam US bond mart.
newsitem.headline: Big Japan-carry-trade unwindings slam US bond mart.

text.p: As talk of a near-term Federal Reserve rate hike increases, the U.S. Treasury market is now at the mercy of large hedge funds, who reportedly have stepped up their unwinding of so-called Japan carry trades.

In recent days, traders said, funds have sold billions of dollars of Treasuries, a prime reason Treasury prices have tumbled and yields have soared. Although selling has been going on for a few weeks as Japanese accounts close their books for the fiscal year ending March 31, traders said the past few days have seen massive unwinding.

"Every day, we have seen waves of selling," said a senior trader at a primary dealership. "They bought billions on the way up and now they are selling billions on the way down. "We are hearing there was quite a bit for sale today."
The trader added that after Friday's morning rally took bond prices up more than a half-point, carry trade unwinding wiped out those gains.

Carry trades, which take advantage of the big difference in yield spreads between high U.S. and super low Japanese interest rates, started picking up steam in September when the Fed left interest rates unchanged.

Because funds figured the Fed was on hold indefinitely with the dollar firming, they saw an easy way to pick up a few hundred basis points and make a bundle of money. As a consequence, the market rallied.
"Now, talk about about a tightening makes it look unattractive," said another trader.

Players noted that large hedge funds believe the dollar is ready to peak against the yen, and with the Japanese economy starting to improve leading to a possible interest rate hike there as well as in the U.S., carry trades are looking less attractive.

Traders said most of the selling has been in short and intermediate issues, primarily in off-the-run two- and five-year notes. They were less sure of where the money is going. Some cited German securities, but there is no evidence of that yet. Others said many of the leveraged funds were keeping the money on the sidelines for now.

"Even with a strong dollar, they are waiting for an opportunity to do something else," said a head trader at a Japanese-based dealership. "It could be these are on a term of three months, and they kept rolling them over. Now, they don't want to roll it over. They want to go into something new."
The problem for the Treasury market is that if these unwindings continue, as many predict, it will be very tough for the market to improve in the short term.
"Retail controls the market," the head trader said. "They are much bigger than dealerships."
